output.title: Before-and-after framing hides the middle
output.body:
The quiet cost of before-and-after framing is that it skips the middle. A small business owner sees “before manual invoicing, after automation” and may get a clean story instead of a clear decision. The middle is where the real work sits: setup, learning, integration friction, and the handoff from a demo into daily use. That is where the spreadsheet gets more honest than the slide deck.

For an owner deciding whether a workflow is worth automating, I would not start with “Will AI do it?” I would start with one recurring workflow and ask whether it is repeatable enough to test. Bareni’s normal sequence is a free 30-minute diagnostic, then a one-page pilot proposal if AI fits. The diagnostic is there to identify the one recurring workflow, say honestly whether AI fits, and define pilot scope, fixed price, and measures. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.

The practical next step is simple: write down one process you repeat every week and define what success would need to show before you commit. Not a vague improvement, but the measure you would actually accept. If you cannot name that in plain English, the “after” is still a story, not a decision.

The real before-and-after test happens inside your workflow, not in a vendor demo.
